Empty means it applies to every type. Note that a MANDATORY STATUTORY INSPECTION is always reported as a clash but is NEVER shifted — its deadline is set by law.
The original due date stays in the "Calendar due date" column. This column is the date suggested after the seasons are weighed — the gap between the two is what to look at.
Applies to every location holding an asset of this category (and of its child categories). Leave it empty and it applies only to the locations named explicitly below.
The number of reading stretches discarded for going backwards or outrunning real time. Above 0 means running hours are UNDERSTATED, and MTBF with them is lower than reality.
Required when the policy is "cannot be done". A bare "forbidden" with no reason will be worked around on site, because nobody knows what they are working around.
The location CURRENTLY holding it. A rotable component may have moved machines during the period — running hours taken from the current location are then an approximation, not an exact figure.
The inspection falls due in %(m)s. It CANNOT be shifted — the deadline is set by law and overrunning it means stopping the equipment. The answer is different preparation, not postponement.
Empty means it applies to every plant. Seasons are local — the Savannakhet wet season is not the Đắk Lắk wet season, so a plant almost always has to be named.

The limit on shifting to avoid a season. Beyond the limit the system REPORTS that the season cannot be avoided rather than shifting further — shifting three months to dodge the rain has already broken the maintenance cycle.
A "cannot be done" rule in season "%s" requires a reason. A bare "forbidden" with no reason will be worked around on site, because nobody knows what they are working around.
Tick it when the counter went back to 0 because the controller was replaced. Only then does the system compensate — otherwise a single typing error pushes back the due date of every hour-based plan.
Empty means it applies to every trade. This is where seasonal rules earn their keep: in the wet season "rope access" cannot be done, while work inside the tower carries on as usual.

Templates attached to every order raised from this plan — a source isolation permit, for instance. Unlike the steps above: a template is shared across plans, so editing it in one place changes them all.

There is a season clash with nowhere to shift to within the limit — or it is a mandatory statutory inspection, which is never shifted. This is the list that has to be done during the season, which means preparing differently.
Work whose due date falls in a season best avoided or one in which it\n cannot be done. The cannot be avoided rows are where\n different working conditions have to be arranged.
A plan falls due on the calendar or on the meter —\n whichever comes first. The Due because of column says which\n one is deciding, so nobody has to guess.
Reliability is a question about the machine: how many\n hours it ran in the period, how many times it failed, and how long on\n average it runs between failures (MTBF).
Declare only day and month, not the year — the window\n repeats itself. A season spanning the new year is\n declared normally: November to March is ONE season.

From the last completion is the right default for servicing: run late once and the next one moves with it. "Fixed anchor" is for mandatory statutory inspections — the deadline is set by law, so doing it early or late leaves the next date unchanged.

A negative number BRINGS IT FORWARD, a positive one pushes it back. For preventive maintenance, bringing it forward is safe while pushing it back lets equipment run beyond its design cycle — so the two directions are not equivalent, and a positive number always carries a warning.

Empty means it applies to EVERY plant. Narrow it down, because each plant has its own vendor service regime, its own machine age, its own O&M contract — one shared plan sweeps a plant still under construction into the maintenance schedule of one already running.

MTTR does not count hours waiting for a crane, for materials, for the wind to drop — that part sits in MDT. The gap between the two is the cost of logistics, not of the fitters' skill; merging them blames the wrong people.

MTBF divides by running hours, not calendar hours: a machine that runs little and fails often looks more reliable on calendar hours than one working hard. Without a running-hour meter, leave it empty rather than substituting calendar hours.
Turn both on and whichever comes first wins — for example every 12 months or 8,000 running hours, whichever comes first. The Due because of column on the schedule says which one is deciding.
This plan runs on the meter only but the location has no reading at all. It will fall silently due, never — not "still in time" but unmeasurable. Enter meter readings for this location.

A season is a window that repeats every year, declared once and used for good. The rules within a season say which type of work is best done, best avoided, or cannot be done — and the maintenance schedule will suggest bringing work forward to escape a bad season, not pushing it back.

pieces of work at this plant fall on the same suggested date. The seasonal rules optimise each schedule on its own and know nothing about how many people the crew has — a pile-up like this has to be spread out by the planner; the system does not spread it.

Used to decide whether to replace or keep repairing, whether to claim under warranty when one batch fails abnormally, and what spares to stock for the things that fail often. This is NOT a scorecard for the maintenance crew — that lives in Maintenance ▸ Maintenance KPIs, read from the same figures.

Maintenance KPIs are a question about the maintenance department: is the repair quick (MTTR), how long is the machine down (MDT), what share of the downtime is sitting waiting, and is the work proactive or reactive (% preventive, % caught early).

There are readings lower than the previous one that nobody has confirmed as a meter replacement. The system applies no compensation to those rows, because a typing error is the likelier explanation — compensating for a typo would silently push back the due date of every hour-based plan.

The steps are copied into the description of the work order when it is raised. The criteria / target value field (tightening torque, clearance, vibration threshold) saves the person doing the work from looking them up and tells the checker what to compare against.

How many pieces of work at the same plant also fall on this suggested date. The seasonal rules optimise EACH schedule on its own and know nothing about how many people the crew has — so work tends to pile up on one date (usually the day before a bad season opens). This column makes the pile-up visible; the system does NOT spread it out, because spreading needs a figure for crew capacity, and that figure is declared nowhere.

MTBF divides by running hours, not calendar hours — a turbine stands still most of the time, and on calendar hours the one that runs least looks the most reliable.
MTTR does NOT include hours waiting for a crane, for materials, for the wind to drop; that part sits in MDT. The gap between the two is the cost of logistics, not of the fitters' skill.

A mandatory statutory inspection is reported as a clash but is never shifted: its deadline is set by law, and overrunning it means stopping the equipment. The answer is different preparation, not postponement.
"Best done in this season" never causes a shift — give it that power and the system would happily push work back three weeks to land in a nicer season, which is exactly the dangerous direction.
